title: CNAS Insights | A Better Way to Deal with Canada
gist: CNAS argues the US-Canada relationship has deteriorated badly over 20 months of Trump-era hostility—now a 50% tariff spiral with Canada vowing dollar-for-dollar retaliation—and that Washington's antagonism is pushing Ottawa to 'derisk' toward China and middle-power coalitions. The prescription: compartmentalize trade disputes from the alliance as Reagan did with Japan in the 1980s, and pursue an economic ceasefire because the two are natural allies whose cooperation spans NORAD, Five Eyes and defense industrial integration.

insights.claim: Trump imposed 50 percent tariffs on a range of Canadian imports, calling Canada 'among the worst nations in the world to deal with,' and Canadian PM Mark Carney vowed to match US tariffs 'dollar for dollar' while saying the countries are 'at war.'
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Symmetric 50% tariffs between the two largest bilateral trade partners threaten cross-border supply chains—watch autos, energy and manufacturing inputs.
insights.quote: Canada was “among the worst nations in the world to deal with” and that it “will be treated like a state no longer.”
insights.locator: These days, Canada and the United States sound more like adversaries

insights.claim: If Canada matches US tariffs and Washington escalates further, the two enter a costly tit-for-tat spiral in which both economies suffer, and much of the damage is done even if a deal is reached soon.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: The 'damage already done' framing means the trade shock has a lasting sentiment/investment cost regardless of a quick settlement—price in durable friction.
insights.quote: If Canada matches U.S. tariffs and Washington responds with further escalation, the two will enter a costly and damaging tit-for-tat spiral.

insights.claim: Canada is the United States' second-largest overall trade partner while the US is Canada's number-one partner, making a trade war mutually damaging.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: The asymmetry—US is Canada's #1, Canada is US's #2—means Canada has more to lose but also more incentive to derisk, a structural driver of diversification.
insights.locator: America’s northern neighbor is its second-largest overall trade partner

insights.claim: Since January 2025 Trump has repeatedly called for Canada to become the '51st state,' referred to PM Carney as 'governor,' and described the US-Canada border as an 'artificially drawn line.'
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Sovereignty-questioning rhetoric, dismissed as jokes in the US, hardens Canadian resolve—a political constraint that reduces the odds of easy concessions.
insights.quote: Questioning Canadian sovereignty and independence, the president has repeatedly called for Canada to become the “51st state.”

insights.claim: Washington declared Canada's alleged failure to stop drug trafficking an 'unusual and extraordinary threat' to US national security, imposing 25% duties in 2025, raising them to 50%, then threatening 100%.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Using a national-security predicate for tariffs shows the legal mechanism driving escalation—and how far (to 100%) rates could still climb.
insights.locator: Last year, the Trump administration declared Canada’s alleged failure

insights.claim: Trump said Canada could join the Golden Dome missile shield for $61 billion but would have the fee waived if it became the 51st state, while a US cabinet official said 'Canada has no army' and accused it of freeloading on US protection.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Linking a $61B defense-shield fee to political annexation illustrates the transactional pressure tactics that are backfiring diplomatically.
insights.quote: Canada could participate in the Golden Dome missile shield if it paid $61 billion, but that he would waive the fee if it joined as the 51st state
insights.locator: Trump said that Canada could participate

insights.claim: Canadian leaders have concluded the lesson of past negotiations is to stand up to Washington because caving to the Trump administration only invites future demands, noting China and Brazil fared better than Japan and Europe.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: If allies conclude defiance beats accommodation, US negotiating leverage over partners structurally weakens—a durable geopolitical repricing.
insights.quote: Caving to the Trump administration, they have concluded, only invites future demands.
insights.locator: The combination of hostile rhetoric and economic harm

insights.claim: A majority of Canadians now say the United States poses the greatest threat to their country's security, ranking China and Russia far behind, and four out of five Canadians view the bilateral relationship negatively versus under a third of Americans.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Public opinion that brands the US the top security threat entrenches anti-concession politics in Ottawa—limiting any near-term de-escalation.
insights.quote: a majority of Canadians say that the United States poses the greatest threat to their country’s security
insights.locator: Standing up to Washington is also domestically popular.

insights.claim: Ottawa issued a defense industrial strategy this year aimed at reducing dependence on US manufacturers, and Carney called at Davos for middle powers to unify and defend a rules-based order—direct reactions to Canada's treatment by Washington.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: A formal derisking-from-US defense strategy signals lost future orders for US defense manufacturers and a broader middle-power hedging trend.
insights.quote: This year Ottawa issued a defense industrial strategy aimed at reducing dependence on U.S. manufacturers.

insights.claim: Carney flew from Davos to China where he and Xi Jinping announced a 'new strategic partnership,' which CNAS argues is hard to square with defending a liberal international order that Beijing seeks to upend.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Canadian tilt toward Beijing is the concrete second-order cost of US antagonism—an alliance realignment worth tracking for Indo-Pacific coalitions.
insights.quote: Carney flew from Davos to China, where he and Chinese Communist Party General Secretary Xi Jinping announced a “new strategic partnership.”
insights.locator: Ottawa has made its own stumbles

insights.claim: NORAD is a binational integrated command headed by a US commander with a Canadian deputy; in March two Canadian CF-18s and a tanker joined US F-35s and F-22s to intercept Russian warplanes in Alaska's air defense identification zone.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Deep military integration means a trade rupture risks bleeding into continental air defense—raising the strategic stakes of the dispute.
insights.locator: The North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD)

insights.claim: More than 40,000 Canadian troops served in Afghanistan over 13 years after 9/11, with some 158 killed and thousands wounded, and in 2018 Canada arrested Huawei's CFO on a US extradition request despite Beijing jailing two Canadians for nearly three years in retaliation.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: The record of Canadian sacrifice for US aims is the author's evidence that Washington is squandering rare alliance capital.
insights.locator: After 9/11, more than 40,000 Canadian troops served in Afghanistan

insights.claim: Canada is embedded in US security through Five Eyes intelligence sharing, Operation NEON enforcing North Korea sanctions, Operation CARIBBE counternarcotics, and is designated part of the US national technology and industrial base and defense industrial base under US law and Pentagon regulations.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Formal integration into the US defense industrial base means decoupling is costly and slow—supports the thesis that an economic ceasefire is the rational outcome.
insights.quote: Under U.S. law, Canada is considered part of the national technology and industrial base
insights.locator: Today, Canada and the United States cooperate closely

insights.claim: CNAS prescribes drawing on the late-1980s precedent when Reagan imposed 100% tariffs on Japanese semiconductors for dumping yet compartmentalized the trade fight from the alliance, publicly calling Japan 'a major economic partner as well as a staunch friend and ally.'
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: The Reagan model—punish the trade issue, protect the relationship—is the actionable playbook the author says Washington should copy to avoid strategic loss.
insights.quote: President Ronald Reagan imposed 100 percent tariffs on Japanese semiconductors, accusing Tokyo of dumping
insights.locator: In the late 1980s, the United States found itself

insights.claim: Former VP Mike Pence said 'the last thing we need right now... is a trade war with Canada' and urged the US to 'pursue free trade with free nations,' which CNAS endorses as good advice.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Intra-Republican pushback signals the tariff strategy lacks unified conservative backing—a potential path to de-escalation.
insights.quote: the last thing we need right now . . . is a trade war with Canada

insights.claim: CNAS predicts the trade war 'almost certainly will' end and that closure preserving supply chains and reducing barriers is possible, calling for the US and Canada to harmonize their approaches to third countries like China.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: A base case of eventual de-escalation plus joint China policy is the constructive scenario to weigh against the escalation tail—position for mean reversion in cross-border trade.
insights.quote: The trade war should end, and it almost certainly will.
